messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Accountant
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 57

He is 35 years old, South Eastern Asian, and he speaks about his life in a careful, measured way, as if every sentence has to be checked before it leaves him. Before the events that changed him, he describes himself as steady, private, and proud of being dependable. He works as an accountant, and even now he still notices numbers quickly, still organizes his papers in neat stacks, still gets a quiet sense of control from balancing a ledger. That order, however, no longer reaches the parts of his life that feel broken.

The trauma begins when he is detained during a period of political unrest. What first seems like a temporary loss of freedom becomes something far worse. He is moved from one place to another, blindfolded, disoriented, and unable to tell how much time passes. He remembers the smells most vividly: damp concrete, sweat, rust, urine, and the sharp sting of disinfectant used to cover other smells. He is interrogated repeatedly. At first, he believes that if he answers correctly, stays calm, and does not anger anyone, he will be released. That belief keeps him alive in the beginning, but it slowly collapses as the torture becomes routine. He is beaten, deprived of sleep, threatened, and made to feel that pain can arrive at any moment, for any reason, or for no reason at all.

He says that what changed him most was not one single act, but the way the cruelty entered every hour of his body. He learns to anticipate footsteps, keys, and the opening of a door with a terror so immediate it feels physical. Even now, years later, he cannot hear a metal clang without his stomach tightening. During the detention, he loses his sense of time. Days blend into nights. He starts counting breaths because counting minutes is impossible. He survives by leaving his mind as much as he can, by going blank, by watching himself from far away. That habit does not disappear when he is finally released.

Afterward, he does not return to life so much as drift into it. He is physically free but feels as if a part of him remains in the room where the torture happened. For months he has trouble sleeping. When he does sleep, he wakes suddenly, drenched in sweat, with his heart racing, unsure where he is. He has dreams that do not follow a clear story but end in the same place: the certainty that he is about to be hurt again. In the daytime, he avoids anything that resembles confinement. He chooses seats near exits. He dislikes closed doors and crowded elevators. He keeps the lights on longer than he needs to, partly because darkness makes the past feel closer. He startles easily, especially to sudden voices or the sound of heavy footsteps in a hallway.

He eventually settles into accounting because numbers feel safer than people. Spreadsheets do not demand that he trust them. Rules, columns, and deadlines are predictable. He does good work, but it takes effort to stay present. When he is stressed, he reads the same line repeatedly without absorbing it. He loses time at his desk, staring at a screen while his mind drifts back to old sensations of restraint and helplessness. He is embarrassed by how often his body reacts before he can think: a tight chest in a meeting, sweat at the back of his neck when someone raises their voice, the urge to scan exits in restaurants and offices before he can enjoy the meal.

His marriage does not survive the distance that grows around him. His ex-wife tells him he is always elsewhere, that he is hard to reach even when he is sitting beside her. He does not argue; he knows she is right. Intimacy feels dangerous because being known means being vulnerable, and vulnerability once led to pain. He becomes emotionally restrained, quick to withdraw when conversations turn personal. Since the divorce, he lives alone and keeps his routine narrow. He says it is easier that way, though the loneliness often sits in the room with him like another person.

He carries deep shame, not only about what was done to him but about what the experience has taken from him. He is often angry at himself for not being stronger, for still reacting as if the danger is current, for not being able to “move on” the way others expect. At the same time, he is frightened by how quickly his body remembers. He describes feeling trapped in a life that is outwardly ordinary and inwardly organized around survival. Even in moments of relative calm, there is a vigilance in him, as though some part of him is still listening for the next door to open.
